She was 18 when 12 men in prison costumes lined up in front of her. She said no. The director said do it. She was paid $4,000 for the shoot. She couldn’t stop crying after. The director didn’t say a word to her. He got his box cover.

Two years earlier she was a cheerleader and field hockey star in Utah. Daughter of a bishop in the Mormon Church. Family of eight kids. Wasn’t allowed to watch The Simpsons. Wasn’t allowed to watch Dirty Dancing. The kind of girl entire congregations build futures around.

Her name is Belladonna. She was born Michelle Sinclair in 1986. At 14 she was molested by an older boy. She tried to take her own life after. At 18 she drove her mom’s car to Los Angeles alone with no money. A recruiter on FetLife told her she could make some extra cash. Her first scene was supposed to be one thing. The director changed it on the spot to something she’d never done. She didn’t know she could say no.

“I didn’t know any better. They lie to you all the time,” she says.

A week later her agent sent her to a real prison set. Twelve men. She tried to back out. He insisted. $4,000. She describes it like a piece of meat thrown into a lion’s cage. 12 lions.

She went home to Utah. Came back a year later. Shot 200 to 300 films. Contracted chlamydia. Started using drugs on set. Had a breakdown. Told a reporter she didn’t want to be alive anymore. Her rate for the roughest scenes was $1,500. The films she appeared in made millions for the studios distributing them. The warehouse worker packing her DVDs got hepatitis B vaccines. She got no health coverage.

In the video below, she sits across from Diane Sawyer and explains what happened in that prison set the way a kid would explain a car accident she was in. Matter of fact. Still smiling. Sawyer asks her why she’s smiling while describing the worst moments of her life. She stops.

“I like to hide my real emotions. I don’t like myself.”

Her mother found out through co-workers who recognized her daughter. She asked herself one question after another. Was it because of the divorce. Was it because she raised her in the church. Was she not rich enough. Was she not humble enough.

She never got an answer.

A Mormon bishop’s daughter from Utah became one of the most recognized names in the roughest side of the industry, was never paid fairly for it, and the only person who asked “did I do something wrong” was her mother.

Did the industry exploit a girl who didn’t know she could say no, or did she walk back into it a year later because nobody on the outside was offering her $4,000 for anything?

The #Ramayana is not a devotional film. It is a devotional force.The hero is not a blue god floating above the story. He is a man who has already seen the end of the world and still willfully chooses to walk into it. 
The rise is not of a kingdom. It is of a mind that challenges weakness. Every frame carries the weight of someone who has burned the old rules and is now moving only by the logic of power . The violence is not spectacle. It is the clarity of consequences
What separates this from every other cinematic telling is that In a time when most films are still wary to move , this one simply moves. It does not explain itself. That is why it hits harder than anything that has come before it.
You do not leave the film having watched a story. You leave it after living an experience

Ranbir In the sequence after Sita’s abduction, when he stands in the empty ashram and simply looks at the place where she was, the camera holds long enough to show that grief has already been converted into a arithmetic
Yash does not play opposition. He plays the mind that has already accepted what it decided to destroy. In the long confrontation before the final night, when he speaks to Ram across the open ground with no army between them, he does not raise his voice. He simply states the price. The face never flinches. The body never shifts.
@AnupamPkher in Jatayu’s  interception of the pushpak is not an act of mere loyalty. Wings half broken, bloodied, he keeps on coming because the mind has not yet accepted what the body is telling it. When he falls, the camera stays on the face. There is no cry. There is only the last argument continuing behind the eyes after his wings have stopped. That is not sacrifice. That is a man who understood the only rule left is to continue until you cannot.

All in all I want to say this to each and everyone of all the greats who collaborated to make this great film is to treat any and all negative critics of this film as barking street dogs against the elephantine effort you all put in to create this magnifique piece of WONDER🙏🙏🙏🙏🙏

Cops found this mom tanning by a pool in Hawaii and handed her a court order: bring your kids back in 5 days. Her 7-year-old son hadn’t been seen in four months. Neither had her 16-year-old daughter. She read it in her bikini, glanced up at the cop and never brought them back:

She knew exactly where they were. That June police dug up her new husband’s backyard. Her son was by the pond, wrapped in plastic. Her daughter was in the family’s “pet cemetery.” The first time police asked about the boy, she said he was at the movies watching Frozen 2:

That was November 2019 in Rexburg, Idaho. JJ, who had autism, hadn’t been seen for two months. Lori Vallow told the officers he was with a friend in Arizona, and that her daughter Tylee was studying at BYU-Idaho. The school had never heard of Tylee. As soon as the police left, Lori called the friend and asked her to send a random photo of some kids. The next day her apartment was empty.

By then three people around her were already dead or nearly so. In July her husband Charles was shot dead by her brother, who said it was self-defense. In October someone fired at the ex-husband of her niece. That same month Tammy Daybell, wife of doomsday author Chad Daybell, was found dead. It was ruled natural, until an exhumation showed she had been asphyxiated. Two weeks after Tammy died, Lori married Chad in Hawaii.

They believed dark spirits could take over a person and turn them into a “zombie,” and that killing that person was the only way out. Lori believed she was a goddess chosen to lead the survivors of the apocalypse. Prosecutors said the money mattered too: life insurance and her kids’ Social Security benefits.

JJ had been killed with a plastic bag and duct tape. Tylee’s remains were so damaged that her cause of death couldn’t even be determined.

In 2023 a jury convicted Lori of murdering both of her children and conspiring to kill Tammy. She got life without parole. Before the judge read the sentence, she stood up and said: “Jesus Christ knows that no one was murdered in this case.” Chad was sentenced to death.

In the video below is the police bodycam from January 2020. Lori and Chad are sitting by the pool in Kauai in their swimsuits, reading the order to bring her kids back. Both children had already been dead for about four months.

Her husband, her two kids and her new husband’s wife, all dead within a year. Who should have stopped her first?
